title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 17 (Copies of memorandum, articles, etc., to be given to members)

content.overview: Section 17 gives a member a statutory right to obtain specified corporate documents on request, subject to prescribed fees. The company must supply the memorandum, articles, and specified section 117 agreements/resolutions within seven days; default attracts a daily penalty subject to the statutory cap.
content.glance: Member requests covered documents; company must supply them within seven days subject to prescribed fees; non-compliance attracts the section 17 penalty.
content.study: Section 17 is a document-access provision. On a member's request, the company must send within seven days, subject to prescribed fees, a copy of the memorandum, articles, and every agreement and resolution referred to in section 117(1) insofar as it has not been embodied in the memorandum or articles. A default exposes the company and every officer in default to a penalty of ₹1,000 for each day the default continues or ₹1 lakh, whichever is less. The provision should be analysed by identifying the requester, the document category, whether the document falls within section 17(1), the request date, the seven-day deadline, applicable fee and any continuing default.

sections.heading: Statutory right and scope
sections.body: Section 17(1) creates a right for a member, on request and subject to prescribed fees, to receive copies of the memorandum, articles, and specified section 117(1) agreements/resolutions not embodied in those constitutional documents.

sections.heading: Seven-day compliance period
sections.body: The company must send the requested documents within seven days of the request. The date of request and evidence of dispatch/receipt are therefore material to compliance analysis.

sections.heading: Default and penalty
sections.body: For each default, the company and every officer in default are liable to a penalty of ₹1,000 for each day the default continues or ₹1 lakh, whichever is less.

sections.heading: Application test
sections.body: Identify the member, requested document, statutory category, fee requirement, request date, seven-day deadline and duration of default before determining liability.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.

enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 17 is a document-access provision. On a member's request, the company must send within seven days, subject to prescribed fees, a copy of the memorandum, articles, and every agreement and resolution referred to in section 117(1) insofar as it has not been embodied in the memorandum or articles. A default exposes the company and every officer in default to a penalty of ₹1,000 for each day the default continues or ₹1 lakh, whichever is less. The provision should be analysed by identifying the requester, the document category, whether the document falls within section 17(1), the request date, the seven-day deadline, applicable fee and any continuing default.

Key statutory components:
1. Statutory right and scope — Section 17(1) creates a right for a member, on request and subject to prescribed fees, to receive copies of the memorandum, articles, and specified section 117(1) agreements/resolutions not embodied in those constitutional documents.
2. Seven-day compliance period — The company must send the requested documents within seven days of the request. The date of request and evidence of dispatch/receipt are therefore material to compliance analysis.
3. Default and penalty — For each default, the company and every officer in default are liable to a penalty of ₹1,000 for each day the default continues or ₹1 lakh, whichever is less.
4. Application test — Identify the member, requested document, statutory category, fee requirement, request date, seven-day deadline and duration of default before determining liability.
